DANGOTE REFINERY IPO: BEFORE YOU BUY, UNDERSTAND WHAT ₦525 REALLY MEANS

September 11 6 min read Latunde Akin

DANGOTE REFINERY IPO: BEFORE YOU BUY, UNDERSTAND WHAT ₦525 REALLY MEANS
Over the past few days, quite a number of clients, friends and associates have asked me what I think about the Dangote Refinery IPO and whether I believe they should invest.
Rather than simply say “buy” or “don't buy”, I decided to look closely at the numbers and share the most important facts I believe anyone considering the IPO should understand.
Because there is an important distinction we sometimes miss:
Dangote Refinery may become one of Africa's greatest businesses and its shares could still be expensive.
Both statements can be true.
That is why I would neither tell anyone to buy this IPO nor tell anyone to avoid it.
I would rather put the important numbers on the table.
WHAT EXACTLY IS BEING SOLD?
As I write this on 10 September 2026, the IPO has not opened yet. It is scheduled to open on 14 September and close on 13 October 2026.
The offer price is ₦525 per share.
The minimum application is 10 shares, meaning you can participate with ₦5,250.
Dangote Petroleum Refinery is issuing 4.1 billion NEW shares.
At ₦525 each, the company intends to raise: ₦2.1525 trillion
Using today's market exchange rate of roughly ₦1,323 to $1, that is approximately: $1.63 billion.
Notice the word NEW.
This is principally an offer for subscription. Existing shareholders are not simply selling 4.1 billion of their shares and taking the ₦2.15 trillion home.
The money raised goes into the company, primarily to support its expansion plans.
Now here is the part many people may not realise
Before the IPO, Dangote Refinery has approximately 120.13 billion shares.
After issuing the 4.1 billion new shares, that becomes approximately 124.23 billion shares.
Therefore, this base IPO represents only about: 3.3% of the enlarged company.
Yes.
For all the noise around one of Africa's biggest IPOs, the base offer represents approximately 3.3% of Dangote Refinery after the new shares are issued.
And there is another interesting detail...
An investment vehicle has already committed up to $400 million, representing roughly a quarter of the 4.1 billion share offer. Once that is spread across the full enlarged company, though, it comes to less than 1% of Dangote Refinery overall.
So the portion genuinely available to the wider market could be even smaller than the headline offer suggests.
If demand exceeds supply, the company is permitted, subject to SEC approval, to absorb up to 30% more shares than the original offer.
So how much does Aliko Dangote actually own?
This also needs clarification.
The approximately 66% you may see beside Dangote Oil Refining Company Limited is not Aliko Dangote's total economic interest.
His disclosed beneficial interest is spread across several entities.
Before the IPO, his disclosed beneficial interest is approximately 87.27%.
After the base IPO dilution, it remains approximately 84%.
So buying shares gives the public economic participation in the refinery
It does not substantially change control.
Aliko Dangote will remain overwhelmingly in control of the company.
For context, NNPC currently owns about 6.8%. So if you have seen a figure around 7%, that is much closer to NNPC's holding than Dangote's beneficial interest.
Now let us talk about the ₦525 price
After the base IPO, approximately 124.23 billion shares at ₦525 imply a market capitalisation of roughly: ₦65.2 trillion
At today's exchange rate, approximately: $49 billion.
Dangote's continuing beneficial interest alone would therefore have an implied value of roughly ₦55 trillion, or approximately $41.6 billion, based purely on the IPO valuation.
That is not cash in his pocket. It is the implied market value of that shareholding.
Now comes the real investment question.
IS A ROUGHLY $49 BILLION VALUARION EXPENSIVE?
On a simple international refinery comparison, it certainly looks rich.
S Oil in South Korea has refining capacity of about 669,000 barrels per day and a current market capitalisation around $13 billion to $15 billion.
HF Sinclair in the United States has about 678,000 barrels per day of refining capacity and is worth about $19 billion.
Tüpraş in Turkey operates about 30 million tonnes of annual refining capacity across four refineries and has a market capitalisation around $16.5 billion.
Dangote has completed performance testing at its original 650,000 barrel daily design capacity and has since processed as much as 700,000 barrels per day, yet the IPO implies an equity value of roughly $49 billion.
On that simple comparison, Dangote looks expensive.
But this is exactly where simplistic analysis should stop.
Capacity is NOT valuation.
Two refineries processing similar quantities of crude can have completely different profitability, complexity, product mix, debt, growth prospects and cash generation.
Dangote also has petrochemicals, access to a huge domestic market, substantial export potential, a relatively sophisticated refinery configuration and plans to expand to approximately 1.4 million barrels per day by 2029.
And the recent financial performance is significant.
The refinery reported approximately $1.82 billion profit in the first half of 2026, compared with a $476 million loss for 2025.
It also generated about $2.6 billion EBITDA during those six months.
That is serious earnings power.
But it raises another question.
How much of that profitability is sustainable when global refining margins normalise?
This is why I would be careful about simply declaring the IPO overvalued.
CardinalStone Research has estimated a 12 month value of about ₦77.7 trillion, with a target price of ₦688.09 per share.
Chapel Hill Denham has estimated fair equity value at about ₦82.6 trillion, significantly above the IPO's roughly ₦65.2 trillion implied valuation.
In other words, some professional analysts looking beyond refinery capacity believe ₦525 could actually offer upside.
They may be right
They may be wr0ng
That is what markets are for.
So what should a serious investor actually study?
• Whether the extraordinary 2026 profits are sustainable
• Free cash flow, not simply revenue or accounting profit
• The approximately $5.67 billion indebtedness reported as at June 2026
• Crude oil supply security and cost
• Refining margins and how sensitive profits are to them
• The execution and financing of the planned $14.3 billion expansion
• Foreign exchange exposure
• Regulatory and government policy risk
• Related party transactions and corporate governance
• Dividend prospects
• Minority shareholder protection
• And ultimately, the return that ₦525 can reasonably produce over your investment horizon.
What should matter much less?
That it is Dangote
That your friends are buying
That people expect the shares to jump immediately after listing
That it is Africa's largest refinery
Or that you are frightened of missing out.
NONE of those tells you whether ₦525 represents good value.
Dangote Refinery is an extraordinary Nigerian and African industrial achievement.
That deserves recognition.
But investment requires a different question.
A great business is not automatically a great investment
A great business bought at the wrong price can become a p00r investment
A r!sky business bought at the right price can sometimes become an excellent one.
So before you ask:
"Do I believe in Dangote?"
Ask the more useful question:
"Do the sustainable earnings, cash flows, r!sks and future growth of this business justify paying ₦525 per share and valuing it at about ₦65 trillion?"
That is the question a serious investor should be trying to answer.
Investment begins where admiration ends and the numbers begin.
Which number in this post changed how you were thinking about the IPO? Tell me in the comments.
- Abiodun Adetula
